projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Margaret M. Lucas was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: This interview is being conducted on Wednesday, July 9, 2008 at Al's Steak House in Joliet, Illinois where we are having our monthly NARFE meeting - that's the National Association of Retired Federal Employees. My name is Fran Prokop and I'll be interviewing Margaret Lucas. Margaret was a civilian employee of the government from 1942 to 1973. We are both officers in our local chapter of NARFE and Margaret heard of the Veterans History Project through me. She has kindly consented to participate in the National Archives Veterans History Project. Here is her story.
Margaret, when and where were you born?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: Jordan Village, Indiana. October 14, 1916.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: What were your parents' occupations?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: My father was originally a teacher and then we had a grocery store - one of those mom and pop grocery stores.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: How about your mother?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: My mother was a piano teacher but she was mostly - well, she always found things to do in addition to being a homemaker.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: What did you do before you began working for the government?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: I worked in my dad's store, primarily.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: How did you enter government service?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: I went to the employment agency and they were hiring; if you knew an adding machine from a typewriter, you were hired.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: Was that in your home town?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: No, it was in Terre Haute, Indiana.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: So your first job with the government was in Terre Haute, Indiana?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: Clerk-typist at the Terre Haute Ordinance Depot.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: When did you begin that job - Margaret has quite a history here and she will be reading some of the answers that she has previously typed up.

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: It was on December 17, 1942. I joined forces at the Terre Haute Ordinance Depot as a Clerk-Typist - CAF-2 - we were known then as CAF; it became GS a little bit later - at $1,440 per year. We worked on Saturdays, which brought the annual salary up to $1,752, which is exactly six dollars per day. I had not taken the examination so I didn't realize that it was Civil Service and that I was going to get 26 days a year of vacation and annual leave, and also 13 days sick leave.

We were classified as "War Service Indefinite" and we had the same privileges. We paid into the retirement fund but no Social Security, of course. I was not a permanent employee until 1948 after I passed the Civil Service Examination and was reached on the register. During the war we were not allowed to use our leave time but it could accumulate to 120 days, which I redeemed later at a GS-12 salary when I retired in 1973. My unused sick leave had accumulated to about one year, which was added to my retirement credits. The only holiday allowed was Christmas; we worked all other holidays at no extra pay.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: What were your hours at that time? Daily hours?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: Eight to 4:30 with a half hour off at lunch.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: And did you say you routinely worked on Saturdays?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: So you worked six days a week during the war.

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: We worked 48 hours.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: That was from 1942 until when?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: Until 1946, after the war - when the war was over.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: And what exactly were you doing from '42 to '46?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: '42 to '46 I was clerk-typist part of the time; then I was into procurement and then I was purchasing agent. In 1946 our commanding officer introduced hosprtalization insurance. A representative from Blue Cross provided information on coverage. Blue Shield had not yet come into existence; it cost 85 cents per quarter. I don't remember when the government got involved and started paying 70 percent of the cost.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: And this was all in Terre Haute that you worked from '42 to '46?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: '42 to '55 in Terre Haute. The installation was a storage depot; we did not manufacture or purchase ammunition or weapons. For some reason it was never abbreviated to THOD; it was always referred to Terre Haute Ordinance. The word "depot" was omitted. We were located at the edge of town in the boonies completely surrounded by railroad yards. We had to leave 20 minutes early in order to get there on time because invariably railroad cars were being switched back and forth barring easy entrance.

Did I mention that gas and tires were rationed during the war so in order to get more than two gallons of gas per week, and retreads, we had to carry riders to work. I did not have a car until 1949, therefore I usually had transportation with someone who lived nearby. Bus fare in Terre Haute at that time was five cents and for an additional nickel we could transfer to a bus to take to the Depot. That was time consuming and undesirable.

The administration building was a two-story wooden building with separate rest rooms and drinking fountains for the "colored." People from Texas had set up the organization bringing their southern customs with them. At the indignation of local employees, the system was abandoned after a few months.

Large open warehouses were also made of wood; everything was temporary supposed to last only ten years. The fact I grew up in my dad's grocery store may have been the reason I was placed in procurement. We purchased items only for maintenance; items in storage were not shipped to the war front. Many items such as paper products and office equipment had to be requisitioned from the Jeffersonville Quartermaster Depot, who would either supply them or give us clearance to purchase them ourselves.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: So that was your job, buy supplies which were sent to servicemen overseas?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: No, no we did not buy those. We bought only the supplies that we needed.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: But what did you send overseas?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: They sent small items, mostly mechanical, overseas; they had pickers and packers in the area.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: And what did they do?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: I don't know for sure what they did, but whatever it was, they did a good job. One of the employees received - I started to say E-mail - but whatever the communication they had at that time, telling them that everything they received from Terre Haute Ordinance Depot was in perfect condition and everything that was supposed to be there was there.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: So you got a communication from them?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: From one of the servicemen. We showed it to our commanding officer and he was thrilled.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: Did you ship out to all services - Army, Navy, Marines?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: No, just the Army.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: You were strictly Army.

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: Strictly Army, yes. It was months before I was given a desk. I worked from a typing table and the arm from the desk besides me. The first year I typed purchase orders from a broken-down Royal typewriter which was exactly like the one used on "Murder She Wrote." It didn't tab property and it was necessary to erase eight carbon copies - if I made a typing error. That wasn't much fun. Purchase orders require many figures to type. And you don't realize when you're learning to type in high school, they don't stress the figures so much -

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: No, you're right; they stress the letters.

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: In the real world you have a lot of figures. Figure typing in high school is not stressed enough, however I did become quite good at it. Now I type figures on my computer instead of using the key pad.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: So you finally got pretty good at it, typing the numbers.

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: Yes. You state you were promoted to purchasing agent; you were shocked that you had to learn to order hardware which included - ha, ha -

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: Yes, I didn't know whether I should put that in there.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: Oh, yeah, are you kidding; they heard worse than that.

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: Yes, I was shocked that I had to order nipples and female and male plugs - and of course the men were taking the orders and it was nothing to them.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: No - and we're talking about the '40s too.

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: Yes, this was in the '40s. We had to send an invoice, a receiving report and a purchase order to Fort Benjamin Harrison (in Indianapolis) for payment. And then we received from the national office, we received something similar to a bank statement, which we had to reconcile. Persons beginning their career now could not imagine the primitive copying system that prevailed at that time. The copy room consisted mostly of ditto machines; copies were purple and operators went home with purple hands and purple spotted aprons; that went on and on.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: I remember ditto machines.

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: After about three years when the war was over our office was combined with the Fiscal Division. In 1950 Indiana State began offering night classes. I returned to college and changed my major from elementary education to accounting and business administration. I was only halfway through my junior year when we were notified that theDepot would be closed; it was closed in December 1955. All buildings were taken over by the Air Force. Many previous government employees remained as contract personnel; most permanent employees transferred to other government locations; about 22 transferred to the Joliet Area. When the divisions combined I learned that my first love was working with figures. Later the divisions were separated; I stayed with Fiscal.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: Now did service men who came back from the war work at these areas?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: Oh, yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: Did they take over some of your jobs?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: Oh, yes; many people got dumped.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: They just got fired outright or were they able to be transferred?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: A lot of times they were able to transfer to different areas.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: But that was the reason all this was taking place because the men came back from the service.

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: The men came back, however, they had no need to keep a depot so they closed it.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: But those men, regardless, those returning veterans had priority with jobs and things.

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: Oh, absolutely. In the Civil Service examinations the veterans, widows and the disabled veterans - there were 10 points added on to their grade. You needed a grade of 70, then they were put at the top of the register. All veterans were given five points, but they had to be reached. But it was nothing short of a miracle the fact that I'm not a veteran that I was able to withstand all of those reduction-in-force layoffs.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: Continuing on with the narrative.

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: That meant that they had to be hired before we could be reached on the register to be made permanent. But I was able, since I had to type all of my own reports, I had no secretary at that time -1 had to type my own reports, so I was able to go back to clerk- typist. You could be reached on the register almost immediately as a clerk-typist. I had to take a demotion to a GS-4 but it was at the same salary - I think it was like 2,770 dollars a year or something like that. And at that time it was a CAF-4 still. I later attained GS-6.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: Was that in the 1950s now?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: That would have been about '46, approximately from 1946, right after the war. The Depot closed December 31,1955. While I was still at Terre Haute Ordnance Depot I attended seminars with personnel at Joliet Arsenal. When they learned the Depot was closing, they offered me a position of GS-6, Budget Analyst with promise of GF-7 within six months. I learned that accounting technician did not qualify me for budget analyst. I had to pass another examination.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: So then you yourself transferred to Joliet?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: Yes, in 1955.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: That was the Joliet Arsenal?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: That was the Joliet Arsenal, yes.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: And what was your job there?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: I had to take the civil service examination to get that job and - I was a little disillusioned with the job because at that time we were just getting the crumbs from OAC - and I had sent over a report to OAC and I had to adjust it. I called and they said, "Oh, we don't use that anymore. We don't even use that." So what I was doing had absolutely no meaning. So after ten years, they closed the Arsenal. The only good part -1 was promoted to GS-11.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: They closed the Joliet Arsenal?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: They closed the Arsenal and I transferred over - it was OAC at that time - Ordnance Ammunition Command, which was later changed to APSA. Due to a water shortage and population explosion, the Munitions Command moved all operations from New Jersey to the APSA location (Ammunition Procurement and Supply Agency) completed in July 1971. APSA was still in operation but my job was absorbed by the Command. The job consisted of budgeting for the maintenance operations of all of the subsidiary plants in the United States. Budget figures were handwritten on a form which was sent to keypunch -

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: I remember keypunch -

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: Since all accounting activities are at the mercy of the calendar, it was necessary to take drastic steps to meet deadlines. Punch cards were packaged and driven to O'Hare to be flown to Washington. Command personnel would meet the plane, thus our deadlines were met.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: If Bill Gates had been around and introduced Windows, I would have had a terminal on my desk. Most of us old-timers were Depression Kids; therefore we were not college graduates. It embarrassed the powers to be that there were some personnel holding positions paying a GS-11 or GS-15 salary with no college credits. As a lot of us were near retirement age, fresh new college graduates were hired at the GS-7 level. They decided to correct this situation.

Lewis University was contacted for assistance. A contract was signed for university personnel to come to APSA during working hours to teach various subjects that could lead to a bachelor's degree. By that time I had credits equal to senior status, so in 1972 I graduated with a BA in the College of Continuing Education with a major in Business Management and a minor in Accounting. The privilege was for statistical purposes only and was not because of job performance. I had received two awards for outstanding job performance. The degree did not provide an increase in pay but it did assist in obtaining a good position later.

Even after building a new Data Processing Building, Washington decided to move the entire operation to Rock Island. On August 29, 1973, I said goodbye to federal service with full health benefits, 120 days of unused annual leave to be paid and one year of sick leave to be added to my retirement credit. Retirement was made with a service of 31 Vi years at Step 9 of GS-11 at a salary of $17,724, which is approximately ten times what I started with as a CAF-2. The salary of $17,724 per annum is equal to a GS-12 salary. Retirement payments consist of about 65% of my last salary. I needed 26 quarters of Social Security to be eligible for minimum benefits. I was young enough and lucky enough to further my career to obtain the necessary service benefits - that's another story.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: So you had 31 1/2 years of federal service.

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: I had 30 and a half and then a year of sick leave.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: And you've been retired now for how many years?

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: Since 1973 - however, I went to work at the Burr Oak Library System as a fiscal manager; I worked there for eight years and retired from there in 1984. I was then eligible for state municipal pensions and Social Security.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: So you had two retirements.

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: And now I have my little business.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: Right, right Margaret is still active. Today she is a very young person and is very active in our NARFE organization; she is our Treasurer and she does have a side business of her own. She has kept very, very busy. She is the first civilian government employee that I have interviewed for this program and it's wonderful - I'm very happy that I got to interview Margaret Thank you, very much, Margaret for the interview and thank you for your service to our country.

sp.speaker: Margaret M. Lucas
sp.p: You're welcome. I enjoyed it.

sp.speaker: Frances M. Prokop
sp.p: Margaret has reviewed her transcript and made minor adjustments, correcting certain facts, etc. after the oral interview was conducted.
